name: Neck posture / forward head correction
lead: Forward head posture (FHP), also called 'text neck', 'tech neck' or 'nerd neck', is a posture in which the head sits ahead of the shoulders, so the earlobe falls in front of a vertical line through the shoulder and the chin appears to poke forward [1][2]. In appearance terms, bringing the head back over the shoulders changes the visible line from chin to neck and the angle at which the face meets the camera, which is why people interested in their profile, jawline and neck contour treat head position as something they can work on without any product or procedure [8][9][17].

Correction is usually described as a mix of habits and exercises: lifting screens to eye level, taking breaks, and strengthening the deep muscles at the front of the neck and the upper-back muscles that pull the shoulder blades back, with exercises such as the chin tuck and neck curl being the ones most often named on looksmaxxing forums [1][17][18]. Clinicians use the same toolkit, under the heading of physical therapy, for neck pain [1].

Most published research on forward head posture concerns neck pain, headache, jaw-joint problems and disability rather than appearance [3][4][5][6][15][26]. A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 cross-sectional studies found that adults with neck pain had greater forward head posture than adults without, but that adolescents did not show a significant difference [6][1]. No published study located for this article has tested whether posture correction changes facial appearance, and on forums the claims run in both directions: some say correcting posture sharpens the profile, others say it makes a recessed chin look worse [8][9][10].

paras: Wikipedia describes forward head posture as visible when the head sits ahead of the shoulders with the chin protruding, usually together with a hunched upper back; the article says that when the person looks up, the upper thoracic curve stays hunched and the lower neck hinges backward, a pattern called 'swan-necking' [1]. Having forward head posture together with rounded shoulders is known as upper crossed syndrome [1][16]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, adds that muscles at the back of the skull and the front of the chest can shorten while the deep neck flexors weaken [2].

The craniovertebral angle, formed between a horizontal line at the seventh cervical vertebra and a line to the ear, is the measure most research uses; a smaller angle means the head is more forward [2][3]. A 2023 systematic review of 26 studies on sagittal head and neck posture reported that the craniovertebral angle differed significantly between people with and without neck pain, while two other measures, the sagittal head angle and a forward-head measure, did not [15].

Wikipedia attributes the recent attention to prolonged hunching over laptops, tablets and phones, which cannot be positioned as ergonomically as a desktop screen, and notes that the iPhone (2007) and iPad (2010) popularised handheld screens [1]. It lists occupations associated with hunched postures, including dentists, surgeons, hairdressers, nurses, chefs and teachers, and medical conditions that increase upper-back curvature such as ankylosing spondylitis, Parkinson's disease and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome [1]. The article cites a 2014 analysis by Hansraj for the idea that neck load rises with forward head position, and gives an estimate of about 10 pounds of extra load per inch; the article itself flags weak sourcing on some prevalence claims [1].

Population studies are older and smaller than the popular discussion suggests. A 1992 study of 88 healthy adults aged 20 to 50 assessed forward head, rounded shoulders and kyphosis against a plumb line and asked about pain [12]. A 2019 study of 50 male laundry workers reported upper crossed syndrome in 28 percent, in a group selected for neck-shoulder pain lasting more than a month [16]. Observational studies have also examined text neck and smartphone use in relation to neck pain in adults and university students [24][25].

Wikipedia outlines a sequence in which thoracic joints stiffen in flexion, mid-back support muscles weaken, the muscles at the back of the neck are strained, the deep neck flexors weaken from disuse and let the chin drift forward, and neck joints are compressed [1]. The article labels parts of this account as unsourced or original research [1]. This is the physiological rationale behind exercise programmes that target the deep neck flexors and the upper back [1][13].

Cross-sectional studies have examined head posture in people with neck pain. A study of 62 patients with neck pain and 52 controls measured the craniovertebral angle and compared it with pain and disability scores [3]. Studies in headache have compared posture and upper-neck muscle performance in people with and without headache [4][5][10][11].

The 2019 meta-analysis found that in adults, a smaller craniovertebral angle went with higher neck-pain intensity and disability, while in adolescents most pain measures were not associated with posture; because every included study was cross-sectional, the authors noted that it cannot show whether posture causes pain or results from it, and called for longitudinal studies [6]. A 2024 randomized trial examined stretching exercises for jaw-joint (temporomandibular) dysfunction in people with forward head posture [26]. These associations concern pain and function, not facial appearance.

Approaches listed by Wikipedia include physical therapy, strengthening of the deep neck flexors and scapular retractors, stretching of tight muscles, ergonomic changes with regular breaks, manipulation, massage, yoga, Pilates and the Alexander Technique [1]. One randomized study of 58 people with chronic neck pain compared two neck exercise programmes for their effect on maintaining upright cervical and thoracic posture during a distracting task [13]. A field study compared neck and shoulder postures of office workers with and without symptoms [14].

No studies found on whether correcting forward head posture, or practising chin tucks or neck curls, changes the appearance of the chin, jawline, neck or facial profile. Related research has examined posture in neck pain, headache, jaw-joint disorders and office work [3][4][13][14][26], including a systematic review and meta-analysis relating forward head posture to neck pain [6] and a 2023 review of sagittal head and neck posture in neck pain [15].

Head and neck posture appears on looksmax.org in several framings. One thread asks whether correcting forward head posture is 'cope', noting that many models and actors have it; a reply suggests they adopt it for photographs to improve their profile [7]. Another poster asks whether years of forward head posture while gaming might have affected maxillary growth [7]. A thread presenting forward head posture as a source of problems throughout the body links to an article and asks for experiences after fixing posture [8].

A separate group of threads concerns chin tucks and neck curls as an exercise pair. One poster asks whether they are 'cope or real' after noticing a small change; a reply says they are not cope 'unless you think it will make you chad', and another poster says the aim is to raise the hyoid area [17]. A poster comparing photos says face fat and body weight were unchanged between them and attributes the difference to weighted chin tucks and improving posture; a reply attributes it to the hyoid bone being raised [18]. Other threads ask whether the exercises make the jaw look wider, and whether realigning hips and neck can fix facial asymmetry [21][22]. A thread on mewing argues that 'adequate neck posture' during puberty would have changed facial development [23].

Some posters say the effect depends on the person's bone structure. One thread argues that a recessed chin or jaw can cause the head to sit forward to keep the airway open, and that tucking the chin back then makes the chin look absent [9]. Another poster says a chin-tuck position makes the voice sound deeper and reports using a posture-based exercise from a voice therapist for puberphonia [19]. The hyoid bone, which these threads mention, is a horseshoe-shaped bone in the front of the neck held in place only by muscles and ligaments and serving as an anchor for muscles of the tongue and larynx; Wikipedia's article on it does not discuss its role in external neck or chin contour [20]. These are community claims, and research on posture and facial form does not clearly address them.

lore.intro: Head posture is discussed on looksmax.org as a profile-improving fix, as a factor that interacts with a recessed jaw, and through the chin-tuck and neck-curl exercise pair that some members say raises the hyoid area [7][8][9][17].

claims.claim: Correcting forward head posture improves the look of the jawline and profile.
claims.believers: Posters describe posture as affecting the whole body and report that good posture becomes natural over time [8]. Others say models adopt forward head posture in photos to sharpen their profile, implying head position changes how the face reads [7].
claims.experts: No published studies have examined whether posture correction changes facial appearance. Published research focuses on neck pain, headache and disability [3][4][6].

claims.claim: Fixing forward head posture can make a recessed chin look worse.
claims.believers: One poster says that with a recessed jaw the forward head position keeps the airway open, and that tucking the chin back makes the chin look absent [9].
claims.experts: No published studies have tested this relationship between head position, airway and chin appearance.

claims.claim: Chin tucks and neck curls raise the hyoid and improve the neck and jaw area.
claims.believers: Posters say the exercises are 'not cope' and the best way to work on the hyoid area, and one shares before-and-after photos with matched weight and face fat [17][18].
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes the hyoid as a muscle-and-ligament-suspended bone anchoring tongue and larynx muscles; no published study located has measured whether these exercises change hyoid position or visible neck contour [20].

claims.claim: Forward head posture in the teen years can affect upper-jaw (maxillary) growth.
claims.believers: A poster wonders whether gaming with forward head posture throughout their teens contributed to their forward-grown maxilla [7]. A mewing thread frames neck posture as part of correct facial development [23].
claims.experts: No published studies have tested posture as a cause of maxillary growth.

claims.claim: Chin-tuck posture makes the voice deeper.
claims.believers: A poster says a held chin tuck made their voice more resonant and describes a therapist-taught exercise used for puberphonia [19].
claims.experts: No published study located has examined chin-tuck posture and voice pitch in this context.

claims.claim: Hip and neck realignment can fix facial asymmetry.
claims.believers: A thread proposes that realigning hips and neck posture can improve facial symmetry [22].
claims.experts: No published study located has tested whether body or neck realignment changes facial asymmetry.

claims.claim: Forward head posture causes pain and other problems throughout the body.
claims.believers: A thread presents forward head posture as harmful beyond the face, citing an article [8].
claims.experts: Cross-sectional studies have found associations between forward head posture and neck pain severity, and a meta-analysis found a correlation in adults but not adolescents; its authors note the design cannot establish causation [3][6]. Headache studies have measured posture in different ways with mixed findings [4][5][11].

card.summary: Pulling the head back over the shoulders to sharpen the profile; heavily studied for neck pain, but nobody has tested whether it changes how the chin looks.
card.aka: Text neck, nerd neck, chin tucks
card.note: Forums disagree on whether correction helps or hurts chin appearance; no appearance studies exist.

quick.overview:
Forward head posture is when the head sits ahead of the shoulders. It is common with heavy screen use and is usually measured with the craniovertebral angle.

Research links it mainly to neck pain and headache. On looksmaxxing forums, people debate whether fixing it improves the jawline and profile or makes a weak chin look worse.
quick.mechanism: Correction usually means postural habits, ergonomic changes and neck or upper-back exercises. Proponents say a better head position improves the visual line from chin to neck; no study has tested this.
quick.risks: Posture exercises are generally low risk and studied in the context of neck pain. The appearance claims are untested, and some forum users report that a chin tuck can make a recessed chin look less prominent.
